summary:
Selangor is a state of Malaysia and stands under the national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish “carnal intercourse against the order of nature” — covering oral and anal sex — with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, regardless of the gender of the participants, whether the act is consensual, or whether it takes place in private. Section 377D adds an undefined “gross indecency” offence carrying up to two years. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records that these provisions have been enforced in recent years, apply to both men and women, are usable against transgender people, and are not confined to Malaysian citizens, so they reach foreign visitors in Selangor.

Selangor maintains its own Sharia layer on top of the federal code. The Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995, like the enactments of all thirteen Malaysian states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, criminalises cross-dressing and “a man posing as a woman”, alongside liwat and musahaqah, with penalties reaching three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences bind Muslims only; a non-Muslim visitor falls under the federal Penal Code alone. Enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the boundary between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground.

In February 2021 the Federal Court struck down cross-dressing provisions of the Selangor Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding the state's legislative power. The judgment turned on which legislature may enact the offence, not on whether criminalising cross-dressing is constitutional, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised as a result. Whether Selangor has since re-drafted the provision within its competence is not covered by the sourced material.

Arbitrary enforcement against transgender people in Selangor is documented. In 2021 Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear in a Selangor Sharia court to answer charges of “insulting Islam” brought over her attire. The state religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced that it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand, where she had fled. She was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia. Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters cite the deployment as evidence of how far authorities will go to enforce rigid gender norms.

Sharia courts in the state have imposed custodial and corporal sentences in these cases: a Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six and seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane. Institutional alternatives to prison are part of the same machinery. At least 1,733 people had attended state “rehabilitation programmes” as of June 2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community that has run since the 2018 election; a 2022 Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters review found such programmes internalise discrimination and foster self-hatred.

Violence against transgender women in Selangor is lethal and largely unpunished. A trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months; reporting on those killings is obstructed, and police mistreatment and impunity go unexamined.

Identity documents remain under state control. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, and a 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holding that sex is fixed at birth and unaffected by reassignment surgery — never gazetted and not legally binding — is applied in practice. A 2016 Kuala Lumpur High Court order directing the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card was overturned on appeal in 2017. There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors, no form of same-sex partner recognition, and no Malaysian law protecting against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern is national, not local. A 2022 Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters review found Sharia investigations and charges covering Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, with state rehabilitation programmes in use across that range. The Federal Court applied the same federalism reasoning to strike down sixteen Sharia provisions in Kelantan in February 2024, again without touching the substance of the offences or the federal Penal Code.

Queuing is no longer required for exposure. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022; a magistrate rejected the police request to extend remand on the ground that no case had been made out under 377B, yet release was delayed and more than 130 detainees were still being held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister said the provisions would be revisited; within days police raided another sauna in Penang. Earlier venue actions include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, and eleven shopping malls in May 2023 over the sale of Pride watches.

Corporal and custodial alternatives to prison vary by state. Terengganu's 2022 amendment extended court-ordered counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution to a year for cross-dressing and other offenders, against a six-month baseline elsewhere; sharia courts may also commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months. Violence against trans women has recurred nationwide, and in July 2020 the Federal Territories Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his “full licence to carry out its enforcement actions” against transgender persons. Official hostility at the top of government is on record: in June 2019 the then Prime Minister told the Cambridge Union that Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage.
localsOnly:
The Syariah offences bind Muslims within Selangor regardless of citizenship. Non-Muslim residents fall under the federal Penal Code only, which means the cross-dressing charge is unavailable against them but sections 377A, 377B and 377D are not.

Residents who are Muslim and transgender face the state religious department's officers directly, including the capacity deployed in 2021 when 122 religious-affairs officers were mobilised for a single case. The absence of any statutory definition of transgender dress means compliance is determined by the officer at the point of contact rather than by a written standard.

Court-ordered rehabilitation and approved-home detention are live sentencing options in the state. At least 1,733 people had passed through state rehabilitation programmes as of June 2021, and the programmes have been assessed by Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters as designed to internalise discrimination rather than to protect participants.

For residents who are transgender and Muslim, marriage is affected: the 1982 fatwa that sex is fixed at birth has been applied in practice to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. The Registration Department's refusal of gender-marker changes affects resident identity cards, bank records, employment and marriage registration, and no court order currently compels it to update markers.

Domestic civil-society infrastructure exists. Justice For Sisters provided bailors and legal aid during the November 2025 mass arrests and works with Human Rights Watch on documentation; in 2021 UNHCR protection was the mechanism that ultimately prevented the return of a Selangor chargee from Thailand.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Selangor re-drafted its cross-dressing provision after the February 2021 Federal Court judgment, and whether any replacement offence is now in force, is unresolved in the sourced material. The inventory confirms the provision was struck down on state-power grounds and that nothing under the federal Penal Code changed; it does not record subsequent state legislative action.

The current status of the 2021 arrest warrant for Nur Sajat in Selangor, and any live proceedings against her, is unresolved. The sourced record ends with her resettlement in Australia under UNHCR protection.

No visitor-specific enforcement data for Selangor is available. The sourced material documents prosecution of residents and of foreign nationals arrested in venue raids elsewhere in Malaysia, and confirms the federal provisions are not limited to citizens, but it does not record a case of a transient foreign visitor prosecuted in Selangor.

Whether the six strokes of the cane sentenced by Selangor Sharia courts are carried out in practice, and under what detention conditions, is not sourced here. The parent framework documents a pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention, but that evidence is drawn from other states.

The count of 1,733 rehabilitation participants is as of June 2021 and no later figure is sourced. The number of people subjected to state rehabilitation since that date, and the number in 2025, is not established.
